and the possibilities to enhance that schedule to be more student-centered. Today, we are outlining our plan to conduct a structured division-wide review of the LCPS middle school schedule. Our goal is to study our current model, gather input from key stakeholders, and explore potential adjustments that better support students and staff. This effort is grounded in feedback that we've received from our principals and our community.

Additionally, it is grounded in our commitment to ensuring student belonging. We really want to look at our schedule and ask ourselves some reflective questions about how can we best meet the needs of our students. Key areas of focus include our bell schedule, elective offerings, student support such as advisory and intervention, and ensuring teachers have meaningful time for collaboration. Ultimately, we aim to develop a division-level framework that provides consistency across schools while

preserving the flexibility needed to meet each school's unique context. We began this work in March by engaging our middle school principals in a thorough discussion of our current middle school schedule. Together, we identify current challenges and establish a clear set of priorities to guide this review. As part of our March discussion, all middle school principals completed a

survey examining key aspects of our current schedule, including structure, service delivery for specialized programs, and elective offerings. Several important themes emerged. A majority of principals, 56%, view the current AB schedule as workable but in need of refinement. There is no single preferred model that emerged. Principals are split between maintaining the AB schedule and moving to a daily schedule, with others suggesting additional

options. Most importantly, principals identified areas where the current schedule does not provide enough time, particularly for student intervention and for flexible, creative scheduling to meet student needs. Two key insights stand out from this feedback. First, our principals, many of them who are here tonight, are deeply committed to strengthening student experiences, especially by

expanding access to intervention, enrichment, and a wider range of electives to meet the needs of all students. Second, they are equally clear that any changes must be carefully aligned with staffing realities. In other words, any meaningful change to the middle school schedule will have direct staffing implications, and the two must be examined together. This balance between innovation and sustainability will be central to our work moving forward.

To ground this work, it's important to understand our current middle school structure. Across 18 schools, we serve nearly 19,000 students in grades six through eight. Under our staffing formula, students take eight classes in grades six and seven, and seven classes in grade eight, with a target class size that aligns with high school at 23.7 students. Middle school teachers teach six of eight periods, with the remaining time reserved for planning, collaboration, and working with students during their resource

blocks. This results in an average student load of approximately 142 students per teacher, close to the state maximum of 150. At the same time, we have limited built-in time for our teacher leaders. Middle school subject area lead teachers teach a full schedule of classes, limiting their ability to attend leadership meetings during the school day, plan for department collaboration, and engage in mentoring and coaching conversations

with department members. Some of these may be important considerations as we think about strengthening our systems to support middle school students and teachers moving forward. This slide provides a side-by-side comparison of a middle school and its feeder high school to illustrate how current staffing and scheduling structures differ across levels. We're using Smarts Mill Middle School and Tuscarora High School as examples. Both schools have similar class size targets

of 23.7 students and comparable enrollment per grade level, 310 per grade level at Smarts Mill versus 352 per grade level at Tuscarora. There are, however, structural differences in how schedules are orga...Middle school teachers are assigned to teach six of eight instructional periods, while high school teachers teach five of eight. This results in an average student load of approximately 142 students per middle school teacher and 118 students per high school teacher.

There are also differences in how staffing supports are allocated. At the high school level, additional staffing is provided to support department leadership. For an example, an allocation of 0.8 FTE for department chair release time in core content areas. Middle schools do not have a comparable allocation within the current schedule. In total staffing, Smarts Mill is projected at 51 FTEs, full-time equivalents, and Tuscarora at 81.2.

These totals reflect differences in enrollment, as well as the way staffing is structured at each level. Overall, this comparison highlights key structural differences in scheduling, and this is important context as we continue this reflective conversation. Based on the survey data and ongoing collaboration, our principal team identified three clear priorities for this work.

One, to enhance and expand elective opportunities, increasing student voice and choice. Two, to strengthen intervention structures, ensuring students have the time and support they need to succeed. And three, to establish a clear, flexible scheduling framework that balances division-wide consistency with school-level adaptability. These priorities will guide our next phase as we explore potential scheduling models and options.
